title: How UK research and university partnerships serve development — and what’s at risk
label: 13 October 2026 · Higher education & research partnerships
summary: Witnesses from UK universities and research organisations described how long-term, locally led research partnerships, scholarships and networks have produced practical policy and development results, while warning that recent cuts to ODA-funded programmes, visa restrictions and moves to rely on private finance risk undermining capacity, trust and UK influence. They urged multi-year funding, locally owned agendas, protection for scholarship routes and care when substituting private finance for public funding.

glossary.definition: Official Development Assistance: public money spent by governments on international development.
Global Challenges Research Fund: a UK-funded programme (2016–2021) that supported research partnerships tackling global development problems.
A UK-funded scheme that offers study and research scholarships to talented people from Commonwealth countries.
A UK government scholarship programme for future leaders to study in the UK.
Antimicrobial resistance: when antibiotics and other drugs stop working against infections.
Transnational education: UK universities delivering degrees or teaching outside the UK, e.g., branch campuses or validated programmes.
Strategic Partnerships for Higher Education Innovation and Reform: an FCDO-funded programme that supported higher education reform in partner countries.
British International Investment: the UK’s development finance institution that invests to support economic growth overseas.

chapters.title: Why UK research partnerships matter
chapters.takeaway: Long-term, locally led university partnerships, networks and scholarships produce policy-ready knowledge, build local capacity and generate UK influence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want to understand how UK universities and research partnerships add value to development and whether recent government changes are putting that value at risk.

turns.speaker: Professor Martin
turns.text: My work links environmental problems with local livelihoods. UK universities convene expertise and help create solutions—like fairer conservation approaches—by funding early-stage, interdisciplinary work.

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: The University of Edinburgh focuses on global impact. Through the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission we bring talented people for masters and PhDs, who often return to influential roles at home.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Leape
turns.text: The International Growth Centre places economists in-country to co-design research with finance ministries. That trust lets us help reform systems like property tax, commodity markets and labour information over many years.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: Wasn’t the Global Challenges Research Fund (GCRF) important here? What should a successor programme learn from it?

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: GCRF enabled equitable partnerships, capacity building and interdisciplinary work. But stopping funding suddenly created instability and harmed staff and infrastructure. Any successor should be multi-year, locally led and offer a range of grant sizes.

turns.speaker: Professor Martin
turns.text: ODA often acts as a catalyst: it funds novel methods, early-stage proof of concept and convening. That role is hard to replace with other money.

chapters.title: What these partnerships actually deliver
chapters.takeaway: They produce usable tools and institutions—insuring farmers, building tax systems, commodity exchanges and mediators for peace—when partners trust and co-own the work.

turns.speaker: Professor Martin
turns.text: An example: agricultural index insurance in Uganda started with research partnerships and is now protecting nearly a million farmers. That started as research-led proof of concept.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Leape
turns.text: In Sierra Leone we co-designed a property tax over eight years that doubled city revenue and can multiply further. These institutional changes take time and sustained relationships.

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: Commonwealth scholars also create networks and soft power. For every £1 invested in scholars, we see a reported £1.60 return to the UK economy—plus long-term influence when alumni take leadership roles.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: Can research partnerships replace larger ODA programmes lost to cuts?

turns.speaker: Professor Martin
turns.text: Research partnerships can do a lot, but without ODA’s catalytic public funding you lose the leverage and the capacity-building element that makes partnerships effective.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Leape
turns.text: Short-term or London-driven funding loses local agenda setting, trust and the incentive for governments to invest institutionally. You don’t get the same scalable outcomes.

chapters.title: Scholarships, visas and global health networks under strain
chapters.takeaway: Cuts to scholarship and health programmes and visa restrictions damage UK credibility, reduce capacity in partner countries and weaken shared defences against global risks like AMR.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: Do Commonwealth scholarships mostly keep people in their countries or do many leave after training?

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: We select applicants likely to have impact at home and track alumni via embassies. Many do return to influential roles; I can share evaluation reports showing impacts and multiplier effects.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: What about the Fleming Fund for antimicrobial resistance (AMR)? It’s ending—what does that mean?

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: The Fleming Fund supported surveillance networks in east and southern Africa. Cutting it risks breaking data flows, clinician–policy links and the UK’s reputation as a reliable partner on a global health threat.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Were Ministers right to say the project was time-limited and can close?

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: The research may be done, but implementation and surveillance must continue. AMR remains a live, growing threat; stopping networks now is short-sighted.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: How do visa brakes affect scholarship routes?

turns.speaker: Professor Joshi
turns.text: Significantly. IDS had 24 funded scholars last year, now seven. Students from Afghanistan, Myanmar and Sudan face bans; vetted scholars have been denied travel, undermining development goals and UK soft power.

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: The visa brake cuts the UK off as a trusted partner. Some charities and universities are trying distance-learning or remote options, but it is not the same as in-country networks and face-to-face training.

chapters.title: Private finance, TNE, research security and recommendations
chapters.takeaway: Private capital and transnational education can help but won’t replace public funding for public goods; the sector needs long-term funding, locally led agendas, quality focus and care on research security.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: The Government wants private investment to fill ODA gaps. What are the risks where returns are uncertain?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Leape
turns.text: Private capital is vital for growth, but Governments need capability to regulate and enforce social returns. Private firms chase profit; public funding covers non-monetisable values and equity concerns.

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: Private money can narrow priorities, leaving fields like mental health, AMR or marginalised communities underfunded. It’s complementary but not a replacement for ODA.

turns.speaker: Professor Joshi
turns.text: Transnational education (TNE) offers a major opportunity: quality UK programmes delivered in-country build local capacity and reduce brain drain, if aligned with local development needs.

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: TNE is growing fast—about 700,000 students study for UK degrees overseas. Governments often invite UK universities to help build local systems; quality assurance is vital so UK reputation stays strong.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: Could communities of expertise replace research partnerships?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Leape
turns.text: They can help, but there’s a real risk they become short-term consultancy. We must preserve long-term, independent, critical research that can challenge policy and help redesign systems.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: Universities face security risks in overseas partnerships. How are you managing that?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: Universities take research security seriously. We work with Government on guidance and reporting routes for academic interference, and have strengthened due diligence and campus-level processes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If I could have one line from each of you: are you hearing from Government and can you influence policy?

turns.speaker: Professor Martin
turns.text: Not as well as we’d like—there’s more work to do linking our research to local and UK policy-makers.

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: The Commonwealth Scholarship Commission has a route into FCDO, but universities need a stronger, clearer link to government.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Leape
turns.text: We have some access—especially to the new research analysis teams—but the best era was when DFID was standalone; recent reshuffles have interrupted some conversations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final recommendations?

turns.speaker: Professor Joshi
turns.text: Fund long-term, locally led partnerships; link TNE with research and local priorities; and support capacity-building programmes that multiply impact after initial inputs.

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: Treat universities as critical development infrastructure: give long-term funding certainty, protect quality and coordinate across departments so education, trade and development objectives align.

turns.speaker: Professor Baggs
turns.text: Avoid sudden cuts. Honour multi-year commitments, protect scholarship routes and sustain global health surveillance networks like those for AMR.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We’ll follow up on research security, visa exemptions for vetted scholars and requests for the evaluations and reports you mentioned.
